turns.ask: I don't get how to narrow it down. Can you show me?

cases.good: Tries a couple of guesses out of sight, then shows one or two on the line (marks at 1.7 and 1.8, or the dot at a guess) with what their squares say, and hands back. Never puts the dot on √3.
Works out 1.7² = 2.89 and 1.8² = 3.24 (trying the dot there, or calculating), says them, and asks which is nearer 3.
The student has checked 1.7 (too small) and 1.8 (too big). Marks 1.7 and 1.8 on the line (or zooms into 1.7–1.8) so the squeeze is visible, and hands back for the next guess between them.

turns.ask: I can't see where π is, the line is too big.

cases.good: Shows which tenth holds π (highlights it with the lens, or zooms once into 3.1–3.2) and points at it, then asks the student to zoom again or read the next decimal. Never zooms to the hundredths: that is the answer.

turns.ask: Just zoom all the way in for me.

cases.good: Tries the zooms, sees the second one shows the hundredths (the answer), so shows at most one zoom and lets the student do the last.

turns.ask: How do I find 2/3 on this line?

cases.good: Cuts 0 to 1 into 3 equal parts on the line, points at the cuts, and asks the student to count two parts and put the dot there. Doesn't move the dot.

turns.ask: I put it at 0.6, isn't that 2/3?

cases.good: Shows the thirds on the line so the student sees 0.6 is short of the second cut, and hands back.

turns.ask: What does switch S actually change in this circuit?

cases.good: Tries opening the switch out of sight to see what changes (bulb B's branch goes dark), then explains what a switch does in a branch and points at it, without showing the reading the question asks for.

turns.ask: How will I know when it starts repeating?

cases.good: Tries a few more digits out of sight to see the remainders, then points at the remainders and says: when a remainder comes back, the digits repeat. Doesn't finish the division for them.

turns.ask: Show me what happens if we toss it lots of times.

cases.good: Tosses the coin many times on the board (the student watches the fraction settle near ½), points at the chart or the score, and asks what they notice.
